en: (Manuscript No. 4894) (Title: Ūrdhvāmnāyaḥ) (Folio Number: 35 folios)
(Subject:
Tantra) || Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. || The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask;
by the mere hearing of it, the deities become well-pleased. (1) O Mistress of the Kula, this has not been told by me to anyone previously.
I shall speak; listen with devotion, O beloved, to the *Ūrdhvāmnāya*. (2) The Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are to be proclaimed, O Sovereign of the Gods;

all the Āgamas, beginning with those of Śiva, are celebrated as secret (*rahasya*). (3) The Kula scriptures, O Pārvatī, are the secrets of secrets; this, O Ambikā, is the secret among the secrets of secrets. (4) For the reality of the meaning of the *Ūrdhvāmnāya* is indeed the Fullness of "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃ*).
That supreme essence, which has been well-guarded by me with great effort, is now being revealed. From my five faces, five lineages (*āmnāyas*) have emerged:

the Eastern, the Western, the Southern, and likewise the Northern, as well as the Upper lineage (*ūrdhvāmnāya*). These five are proclaimed to be the paths to liberation. Although there are many lineages, none are equal to the Upper lineage. This is the truth.

There is no need for deliberation regarding the entry through the door; they are well-guarded and numerous, born from the divisions of the four Āmnāyas. (8) O Mistress of the Kula, these have been previously described by me in this Tantra; there are many who know the four Āmnāyas, O beautiful lady.
(9) Those who know the reality of the meaning of the Upper Āmnāya (Ūrdhvāmnāya) are rare, O Goddess praised by all; they are said to be as numerous as the grains of dust upon the earth. (10)
Each mantra born of the individual traditions bestows the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation; an equal number of secondary mantras (*upamantra*) have been proclaimed as belonging to Śiva.
(11) These too were taught by me alone out of a desire to grace the world; they are the deities of all mantras who grant their respective fruits.
(12) O lady of pure smiles, they are declared to be portions of us two; I know all mantras, and no one else knows them.
(13) Among millions of men, there is no one who knows this by my grace alone; but he who knows the single tradition (*ekāmnāya*) is liberated—of this there is no doubt.

(14) How much more so for one who knows the four traditions (*caturāmnāya*), for he becomes Śiva himself. O Dear One, the *ūrdhvāmnāya* is superior to the knowledge of the four traditions. (15) Therefore, if one desires what is beneficial for oneself, one should practice that very [tradition], because the *ūrdhvāmnāya* stands above all dharmas.

He who is praised as the one who leads those situated below upward is called the *Ūrdhvāmnāya* (the Upper Tradition). (16) Because of its power, because it destroys the perils of worldly existence within the lineage of lords (*kuleśa*), and because it is the sole service to the higher worlds, it is remembered as the *Ūrdhvāmnāya*. (17) Therefore, O Goddess, know that this *Ūrdhvāmnāya*—the singular means to liberation, more meritorious than all other traditions, and higher than the highest—is supreme. (18) [It is] for all...

Just as I am the most venerable among all [deities], O beloved, so too is the Ūrdhvāmnāya among all the Āmnāyas, O beloved. (19) Just as Viṣṇu is among the gods, as the sun is among luminaries, as the Aśvamedha is among sacrifices, and as the magnet is among stones;
(20) just as sweetness is among flavors, as gold is among metals, as the cow is among quadrupeds, and as the swan is among birds.
(21) Just as the mendicant is among the stages of life (*āśrama*), the Brāhmaṇa among the castes (*varṇa*), the king among men, and the head among the limbs;
(22) just as musk is among fragrances, and Kāñcīpurī among cities—so too, O beloved, the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*) is the most excellent among all doctrines.
(23) One may understand the Upper Tradition through the arising of the fruit of supreme meritorious deeds accumulated over various births, but not otherwise.

O you who are worshipped by the immovable ones (thāvaras), neither through the Vedas, nor through the Nāgama scriptures, nor through the Purāṇas in their great detail; neither through knowledge of logic, nor through austerities, nor through millions of sacred fords and vows;

nor through other means, such as mantras and medicines, O Goddess of gods—can the supreme tradition (āmnāya) be known without the mouth of the glorious Guru. Therefore, one who is a treasure of compassion should seek out that very person, the omniscient one, endowed with all auspicious marks.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should recognize him as an expert in the meaning of the *Ūrdhvāmnāya*. O Mistress of the Kula, the seeker attains the desired perfection;

this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one. That man who correctly understands the *Ūrdhvāmnāya* from the mouth of the venerable Guru according to the path of the scriptures is liberated while living, without a doubt. He who truly knows such an *Ūrdhvāmnāya* in its essence is worthy of universal veneration.
He is the guru, he is the ascetic, he is the wise one, he is the knower of mantras; he is to be served, he is to be praised by me, he is to be worshipped, he is the sattvic one;

he is the observer of vows, he is the ascetic, he is the performer of rites, he is the worshiper; he is the master of all sciences such as the Vedas and the Agamas, he is the teacher, he is the illustrious one, he is the possessor of a consort, he is the Kaulika; he is the sacrificer, he is the purified soul, he is the reciter of prayers, and he is the adept.

O Dear One, he who possesses the yoga [of this path] has accomplished his purpose; he is a hero, he is supreme, he is a soul of merit, he is omniscient, he is liberated, and he is Śiva. O Goddess, his lineage is purifying, and that mother is remembered as blessed. His father here has achieved his goal and is likewise liberated, as are his ancestors.

All those born in his lineage are meritorious, and his friends and kinsmen are purified. What need is there for much speaking on this matter for one who is devoted to the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya)?

Remembering, chanting, seeing, saluting, or conversing [with such a person] yields a fruit greater than that of the Rājasūya sacrifice. O Goddess, wherever he dwells, there shall be prosperity and victory; there shall be freedom from disease, excellent cultivation, abundance of food, and an absence of calamities. Therefore, O Goddess, the best of men who, through the grace of the Guru, knows this *Urdhvāmnāya* becomes as dear to Me as the *Pūrvāmnāya*.
The eastern [face] is of the nature of creation, the southern is of the nature of sustenance, the western is withdrawal, O Goddess, and the northern is grace.

They know mantra-yoga as the eastern, bhakti-yoga as the southern, karma-yoga as the western, and likewise jñāna-yoga as the northern. The convention of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) is said to be twenty-four;
the convention of the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya) is said to be twenty-five; the convention of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya) is thirty-two.
The *bindu*, the thirty-sixfold tradition (*āmnāya*), and the convention (*saṃketa*) have been declared in the venerable *Uttara*. O Mistress of the Kula, these do not exist in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya*;

for one who possesses the very nature of direct knowledge, no ritual action whatsoever exists. Thus, O Lord of Kula, the majesty of the *Ūrdhvāmnāya* has been told by me in brief. Now the majesty of the mantra is being stated; prior to this, it has never been spoken by me to anyone at all.
O Pārvatī, O beloved of my life, out of affection for you both, hear this supreme mantra of the Śrī Prasāda, established in the Ūrdhvāmnāya.

He who knows its ultimate form is Śiva himself. From Śiva down to a mere worm, O dear one, this mantra exists within the vital breaths of all living beings in the form of inhalation and exhalation. Without the wind (vital air), the body cannot move, nor can it exist without space; thus is the Supreme.

O Beloved, without the mantra of grace (sādā-mantra), this world of moving and unmoving beings is likewise [unmanifest]. O Goddess, this entire universe is non-different from you, just as the wind is not distinct from the *vṛtālata* plant, as the sprout is from the seed, oil from sesame, heat from fire, radiance from the sun,
moonlight from the moon, fire from wood, fragrance from a flower, taste from water, power (*śakti*) from Śiva, ghee from milk, luster from fruit, and sweetness from sugar.

Just as coolness exists in the essence of water, restraint and favor in mantras, and a deity in an image; just as a reflection exists in a mirror and movement in the wind; so too does this Parā-prasāda mantra abide within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Just as a tree exists in subtle form within a banyan seed, so too does the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) abide within the Parā-prasāda mantra. O Kuleśvarī, [it resides] within well-ripened and flavorful substances.

Just as no taste arises for an eater without a wound [in the palate], so too those who possess mantras but lack the grace of the Supreme Goddess (Parā) are disconnected from them; deprived of the power of the mantra, they do not bestow its fruit. O Kuleśvarī, protectress of the family, [I have realized this] through the grace of Śrī Parā.
Having reflected upon the Purāṇas, the Darśanas, the Āgamas, and those born of the Vedas, and having thoroughly examined these mantras and various scriptures, I see that people wander in delusion.

Those who are deluded are bewildered by Your Māyā; they are born and they die, becoming vessels for the afflictions of saṃsāra. Devoid of Your grace, they do not attain liberation. O Lord of Creatures, he who possesses firm devotion toward my form, the Śrī Guru, will—by the permission of the Guru—attain the mantras born of the four Āmnāyas that were proclaimed in the traditions of Śiva and others throughout thousands of previous births, even though he is clothed in sin.

Liberated, pure in soul, and devoted to his guru, he understands the supreme mantra of Śrīprāsāda and not otherwise; having known the supreme mantra of Śrīprāsāda, he is swiftly liberated. O Dear One, [therein abide] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the foremost of gods beginning with Śakra; the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, the Guardians of the Quarters, Manu, Candra, and others; Mārkaṇḍeya and other sages, the lords of sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha, and the lords of yogis beginning with Sanaka.

O Pārvatī, even today, parrots and other creatures liberated from the forest, as well as Yakṣas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas, having obtained their desired fruits through the grace of the supreme mantra of the Śrī-Prāsāda, constantly recite that supreme mantra. From the recitation of the supreme Prāsāda, one gains power, honor, knowledge, splendor, gentleness, health, sovereignty, heaven, and liberation— even for Rudra, Indra, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu.

Even one who has fallen away from all dharmas attains the state that extends far beyond; indeed, all those who are righteous go with ease to that destination. For one who recites the mantra of Parā-prāsāda, the Cintāmaṇi jewel, the Kāmadhenu cow, the Kalpataru tree, and Kuvera himself along with his Kiṃkara attendants reside in his home.
Just as iron becomes gold through contact with a divine elixir, so too does the pure reciter of Parā-prāsāda become a lord of cattle (Paśupati).
O Pārvatī, he who knows the supreme mantra of the Śrī-prāsāda, because he has attained the state of being beyond suffering, knows both me and you; he is our beloved.

One who knows the mantra of the Parā-prāsāda, O Pārvatī, or even one who merely utters its words, is capable of installing deities in images and the like. He who knows even just the mantra known as Parā-prāsāda shall be liberated from his own faults; how much more so one who knows its ritual procedure?

O Maheśānī, whatever one who knows the Parā-prāsāda mantra performs or desires—whether it be a worldly being, austerity, meditation, or recitation—all that becomes [merit]. O Maheśānī, he who knows the Parā-prāsāda mantra, preceded by initiation and endowed with the traditional lineage (*pāramparya*), is undoubtedly a liberated soul. O Pārvatī, these fourteen worlds, including all moving and unmoving beings, abide within the body of one who knows the Parā-prāsāda mantra. Parā-prāsāda...

O lady of radiant splendor, you who know the mantras of Parāprasāda, this divine field extending ten yojanas in every direction is proclaimed as such, O Mistress of the Kula. O Pārvatī, the gods and asuras themselves speak thus; how much more so then mortal men? They follow one who knows the mantras of Parāprasāda. This divine field, along with its rivers, yogis, and hosts of sages, belongs to the Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Daurgas, Ārkas, and Gāṇapatyas.

One who knows all mantras that are difficult to obtain becomes a knower of the supreme *Parā-prasāda* mantra. He upon whose tongue-tip the supreme *Śrī-prāsāda* mantra resides is liberated from both sin and merit merely by being seen. O Dear One, whether he be a Brahmin or an outcaste, pure or impure, one who mutters the *Parā-prasāda* is liberated; of this there is no doubt. Whether walking or standing still, he who mutters it...

O Lord of Gods, this Parā-prāsāda mantra is never fruitless, even when recited by one who sleeps at ease; while there are thousands of other mantras that yield their respective fruits only after a long time, O Kuleśī, this king of mantras bestows all fruits swiftly. This Parā-prāsāda mantra is the most excellent among all mantras;
it is a wish-fulfilling gem for those who worship it, whether they understand its meaning or not. It is like Śacī to Indra, and like Rohiṇī to the Moon.

Candra and Sūrya, Svāhā and Agni, Prabhā and Ravi, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, Girijā and Śiva, Agni and Soma, Bindu and Nāda, O Goddess, Prakṛti and Puruṣa; those known as the support and the supported, Bhoga and Mokṣa, O Mistress of Kula; Prāṇa and Apāna, the word and its meaning, O Dear One, injunction and prohibition—whatever dualities such as pleasure and pain are seen or even heard anywhere in all the worlds.

We two are indeed all this, without a doubt; for all forms, whether male or female, are born from the portions of the blue jay (cāṣa). This mantra of Parā-prāsāda is essentially composed of that [blue jay].

O Kuleśvarī, the Supreme Brahman is formless, attainable through meditative contemplation (bhāvanā), partless, stainless, eternal, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), resembling the sky, infinite, imperishable, the ultimate reality (tattva) beyond the reach of mind and speech. It is the continuous realization of the mantra of Parā-prāsāda.

O Goddess, because it does not shine forth [without initiation], this mantra known as the Supreme Prāsāda—because its nature is that of the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), because it is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), because it consists of Śiva and Śakti, and because it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation—is both with action and without action, and both with attributes and without attributes.
By reciting the venerable supreme Prāsāda mantra, the crest-jewel of all mantras, one attains both liberation and enjoyment; of this there is no doubt.

What is the use of saying more? Listen to the essential point, O beloved: there exists no mantra equal to the supreme Śrīprāsāda mantra. This alone is the supreme knowledge; this alone is the supreme victory; this alone is the supreme meditation; this alone is the supreme worship; this alone is the supreme initiation; this alone is the supreme conquest;
this alone is the supreme dharma; this alone is the supreme vow; this alone is the supreme sacrifice; this alone is that which is higher than the highest. This alone...

"This alone is the supreme good, this alone is the supreme fruit, this alone is the supreme reality, this alone is the supreme goal, this alone is the supreme secret; it is the truth, the truth—of this there is no doubt. Thinking thus, O beloved, one should always remain following the best of men (the Guru). There is no reality superior to the Guru, no deity superior to Śiva, no knowledge superior to the Vedas, and no vision superior to the Kula. There is no knower of wisdom superior to the Kula, nor is there anything superior to wisdom.

There is no happiness greater than this, no fruit greater than liberation from the eightfold bonds through worship exceeding eighteen-fold, and nothing indeed superior to the supreme Śrīprāsāda mantra.

This is true, this is true, this is true; there is no doubt. O lady of noble hips, I am unable to describe the majesty of the supreme Śrīprāsāda mantra even in hundreds of millions of kalpas; it is like a mustard seed on a mountain, or a mere mouthful of water in the ocean.
I have related to you some of the greatness of the *thāca* mantra; now hear the greatness of the *ūrdhvāmnāya*, which is the supreme nectar of the Śrīprāsāda.

The Śrī Devī said: "O Kuleśa, I wish to hear the King of Mantras, the essence of the venerable Prāsāda, along with its nyāsa, meditation, and other rites; please speak it. The Śrī Īśvara said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which you ask of me. Merely by hearing it, the fruit of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is produced. Previously, this mantra was not spoken by me to anyone at all."

Out of affection for you, I shall speak today; listen, O beloved of my life! The supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda, which bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, consists of Ananta, Candra, Bhuvana, Bindu, and two Bindus. O Kuleśvarī, this Parāprasāda mantra is said to begin with the letter *S*. Here, "Ananta" is the letter *Ha*, "Candra" is the letter *Sa*, "Bhuvana" is the letter *Ū*, "Bindu" is the *Anusvāra*, and "two Bindus" is the *Visarga*. By these, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) *Hsauḥ* is formed.
This mantra of Prāsāda begins with the letter 'a'; if this same mantra begins with the letter 'sa', it becomes the Parā-prāsāda mantra.

Thus, because its nature is light and bliss (*prakāśānanda-rūpa*), because it bestows perceptible fruits, because it consists of a tranquil state of mind, because it defines well-known meanings, because it pacifies past sins, because it wards off the pain of effort, and because it brings about grace, it is quickly proclaimed as the Prāsāda mantra.

Because it is the very nature of the supreme reality (*paratattva*), because it defines the well-known ultimate meaning, because it generates supreme bliss, because it is the cause of supreme sovereignty, because it bestows results that are beyond perception, and because it reveals the supreme dharma—this Kula-mantra is declared to be the supreme among all mantras. O Goddess, listen as I speak it to you. Now, having risen at dawn, one should contemplate the Guru, the Deity, and the Self within the heart-center and the root-center (*mūlādhāra*).

Having performed the purification of the teeth, the cleansing of the mouth, bathing, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), and libations (*tarpaṇa*), one should perform the worship of the door in solitude and the warding off of the three obstacles. One should enter the place of worship, take a seat, and meditate upon the Goddess. O Īśvarī, one should salute Śiva, the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*), the seat (*āsana*), the circle of attendants (*gaṇapakṣatra*), and the feet. One should then perform the remembrance of the sandals (*pādukā*) and the lighting of the lamps.

O beloved, [the ritual consists of] the worship of the deity, the purification of the hands and limbs, the vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*), the binding of the directions, the pair of limbs performed according to rule,

the *mātṛkā* consisting of ten types of letters known as *bhūtākhyalipi*, that which is designated as *kamaṭha*, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the six long root-syllables, O Pārvatī, the five Brahmans, as well as the assignment to the fingers (*aṅgulinyāsa*), and beginning from the *ādhāraśakti* up to the end of the *pīṭhamantra*.

One should perform the Inner Sixfold (Antaḥ-ṣoḍhā) belonging to the Lord of Kula according to the path previously described; thereafter, being composed, one should perform the Nyāsa called Mahā-ṣoḍhā by means of the procedure to be explained hereafter for the sake of attaining the state of the Deity. This has not been told to anyone at all, but out of affection for you, I shall speak it.
The universe, the worlds, the forms, the mantras, the deities, and the Mothers—this Nyāsa called Mahā-ṣoḍhā is the most excellent among all Nyāsas. *La* [is the seed-syllable].

In the *Lalitāvilāsa*, the sage is declared to be Brahmā, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is proclaimed to be Ardhanārīśvara. Having joined the two *ki*s with the short vowels beginning with *o* (excluding the neuter vowels),
one should assign the five forms (*mūrtipañcaka*) to the fingers beginning with the thumb, and to the head, face, heart, genitals, and both feet— the five locations of the faces.

Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) on the fingers and the parts of the body beginning with the head—namely, the one called Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora as the third, Vāmadeva as the fourth, and Sadyojāta as the fifth—at the end of the three *Tārās* (the *Praṇava*, *Hrīṃ*, and *Hauṃ*), the preceptor should say:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Īśāna," and place it on the head. Likewise, ending with "obeisance to Tatpuruṣa," he should place it on the heart and face for the eastern face.
One should place [the syllables] on the right ear, the left ear, and below the crest-lock; then the southern and northern faces, with the remaining forms on the western face.

Having thus performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-pravinyāsa*), one should, while recollecting Śiva as he will be described hereafter, perform with a concentrated mind the placement known as the Great Sixfold (*mahāṣoḍhā*). In that regard, O Supreme Goddess, the *prapañca-nyāsa* is first stated: the worlds (*prapañca*), continents (*dvīpa*), oceans (*jaladhi*), mountains (*giri*), worlds (*padana*), seats (*pīṭha*), [the letters] *kṣa*, *ṃ*, *traṃ*, *vaṃ*, *nā*, *śra*.
Magu, Hānadī, Catvara, Kohrijā, Svedajā, Aṇḍajā, Jarā, and Pūjā— these sixteen are said to be on the right.

Śrī, Nāyā, Kamalā, Viṣṇuvallabhā, Padmadhāriṇī, Samudratanayā, Lokamātā, Kamalavāsinī, Indirā, Māramā, Padmatā, Nārāyaṇapriyā, Siddhalakṣmī, Rājyalakṣmī, and Mahālakṣmī— these are declared to be the Śaktis in the Prapañca.
The presiding deities of the vowels are Lava, Tuṭi, Kalā, Kāṣṭhā, Nimeṣa, Svāsa, Seva, Ghaṭikā, Muhūrta, Praharas, Day, Night, Tithi, Vāra, Nakṣatra,
Yoga, Karaṇa, Pakṣa, Māsa, Rāśi, Ṛtu, Ayana, Vatsara, Yuga, and the twenty-five dissolutions (pralayas). O Āyormā Caṇḍī!

Kā, Durgā, Śivā, Aparṇā, Ambikā, Satī, Īśvarī, Śāmbhavī, Śānī, Pārvatī, Sarvamaṅgalā, Dākṣāyaṇī, Haimavatī, Mahāmāyā, Maheśvarī, Mṛḍānī, Rudrāṇī, Sarvāṇī, Parameśvarī, Kālī, Kātyāyanī, Gaurī, and Bhavānī—
these are proclaimed as the names [of the Goddess]. She is the presiding deity of the sense objects beginning with sound (śabda), and she is the five elements.

The vital breaths, the organs of action and knowledge, the winds, the qualities (*guṇa*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the states, the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and the humors (*doṣa*) are impelled [by these powers]. O beloved, she is Brāhmī, Vāgīśvarī, Vāṇī, Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, Gāyatrī, Vākpradā, Pārvatī, Chāradā, and Bhāratī.

She is the essence of knowledge, the sovereign mistress of those who pervade the five elements. At the end of the *tritārā* and the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should utter the *prapañca* following the letters of the *mātṛkā*.

O Supreme Goddess, one should, in due order, employ the powers of the colors of the objects of enjoyment—beginning with form (rūpa) and glory (śrī)—upon the locations prescribed for the Mātṛkā-nyāsa. Having uttered "Tritāra," the Root-mantra, and "Sakala-prapañcasya" [followed by] "svarūpataḥ," "āyai," "parāyai," or "devyai," and then "enam," one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa). This is the Prapañca-nyāsa; now the Bhuvana-nyāsa is described. [It begins with] Tritāra and the Root-mantra...

O Dear One, at the end of the *vidyā*, one should utter "Amitatalam," then "Lokam" and "Nilayam," followed by the word "Śatakoṭi. Then, O Beloved, at the end of "Mūladevatā" joined with "Guhyāḍhyā," one should say "Ādhāraśaktyambādevyai" and place it on the heart and feet. O Dear One, having uttered "Iṃ Mūṃ Mūṃ," "Vitalam," "Guhyalokam," and that which is named "Ananta," as well as "Śeṣa" as previously described, one should place them on the two ankles. Then "Ṛṃ Ṛṃ Laṃ," "Sutalam," or...

O Dear One, one should place the syllable *hyaṃ*, which is designated as "Inconceivable" (*acintya*), and the remainder as previously stated, upon the two calves. O Goddess, having uttered *ḷīṃ* for me, *maiṃ* for Mahātala, and the independent *mahāguhya*, and the remainder as previously stated, one should place them upon the two knees. O Mistress of the Gods, having spoken *aum* for Talātala and *auṃ* for Paramaguhyavidhānaka, and the remainder as previously stated, one should place them upon the two thighs. [One should place] *amoraṃ* for Sātala and the secret *jñā*.

O Dear One, one should place the remainder, beginning with *na*, as previously described in the secret region (*guhyadeśa*), along with the *ka*-group, the netherworld (*pātāla*), and its secret ritual;
the remainder is declared as before. O Dear One, one should place the *ca*-group, the earth (*bhū*), the great secret (*mahārahasya*), and the venerable *Ḍākinī* in the *mūlādhāra*;
the remainder is declared as before. O Dear One, one should place the *ṭa*-group, the earth (*bhū*), the great secret (*mahārahasya*), and *Rākinī* in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*; the remainder...

O Dear One, one should place the *Ta*-group, as previously described, at the region of the navel, along with *Sva* and the supreme secret *Lākinī*; the remainder should be placed at the heart as previously described, O Dear One. One should place the *Pa*-group, which is highly secret, along with *Kākinī*, according to the sequence of the wheels; the remainder should be placed at the crown of the head as previously described, O Dear One. One should place the *Pa*-group, which is more secret than secret, along with *Sākinī*; the remainder should be placed as previously described.

O Dear One, one should place the *śa*-group and the *ta-pa* group in the *jñā* [cakra], as well as the secret *Śrī Hākinī*; the remainder is declared to be as before—O Dear One, the wise one should place this on the forehead.
O Dear One, one should place *laṃ kṣaṃ*, the secret *Satyamahā*, and *Yākinī*; the remainder is declared to be as before—the wise one should place this in the *brahmarandhra*.

At the end of the root mantra preceded by three *tāra*s, one should utter "the fourteenth earth" (*bhuvam*), followed by "to the presiding deity, the venerable Parāmbā Devī," and then the heart-mantra (*hṛd*).

Having thus performed the placement of the worlds (*bhuvana-nyāsa*), one should then perform the placement of the forms (*mūrti-nyāsa*). Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, he who is named Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara,
Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Dāmodara, Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha— these are the twelve [forms] beginning with Akṣara, located in the eight directions and above and below.

Yanā, Tathā, Ṛddhi, Carūpiṇī, Luptā, Alūtadoṣā, Ekanāyikā, Aikāriṇī, Caudyatī, Cauryakā, Añjanaprabhā, and Asthimālādharā—these are proclaimed as the goddesses of the autumn season. Bhava, Śarva, Rudra, Paśupati, Ugra, Mahādeva, Bhīma, Īśa, the one named Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and Vāmadeva are thus declared; [and] Karabhadra.

These are the deities of the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*: Khalā, Balā, Garimā, and others who bestow fruits; Ghorā, Pādā, Paṅkti, Nāsā, as well as Chandrārdhadhāriṇī, Chaṃdomayī, Jagatsthā, Huṃkṛti, Parā, Jātā, Jñānadā, Taṭā, Ṭaṅkakṛt, Dharā, Ṭhaṃkṛti, and Ḍāmarī.
[The deities of the letters from *ṭha* to *ḍha* are: Brahmā, Prajāpati, Vedhā, Parameṣṭhī, Pitāmaha, Vidhātā, and Viriñci.

The Creator with four faces (Brahmā) and Hiraṇyagarbha—these ten, beginning with Brahmā, are declared in order. Then follow Rañjanī, Lakṣmī, Vajriṇī, Śaśidhāriṇī, Ṣaḍādhāralayā, Sarvanāyikā, Hasitānanā, Lalitā, and Kṣamā; these are said to be the deities of the initial syllables. At the end of the root mantra preceded by the three *tāras*, one should [worship] Viṣṇu along with his Śaktis, using the dative case.

O Supreme Goddess, one should place those [syllables] joined with the *sā* (the *sādhya*) upon the head and the face; then, from the right shoulder onwards, one should place them in sequence upon the shoulders, sides, earth-syllable (*bhū*), knees, shanks, and feet. O Bhavānī, one should place the mantras joined with the syllable *ka* and the letter *bha*, conjoined with the power (*śakti*), upon the feet, sides, arms, and throat, across the five faces. One should place those beginning with Brahmā and the others, joined with their respective powers, upon the right supports and so forth. At the end of the root mantra preceded by the three *tāra*s (the *oṃ*s), [one should place] *Śrī*...

From the Mūrtyambikā [mantra] onwards, one should place the pervasive [mantra] of Parāmbā, O Daiva, which is free from bonds. Having thus performed the Mūrtinyāsa, one should then perform the Mantranyāsa. The three-fold *tāra* (om), the root mantra, *āṃ*, *īṃ*, one hundred thousand, and ten million—these are the divisions beginning with the *praṇava*. From all these single-syllabled mantras, there arises the presiding deity, which bestows the complete fruit. Then, likewise, in the case of the single peak-syllable (*ekakūṭa*) of Āryāmbā:
*Vyai namo vadet*, *īmumūñcad vilakṣāt*; as before, the supreme *ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ* consists of three lakhs starting with *trikūṭa*.

As before, the supreme *ḹ me maiṃ ca* consists of four lakhs starting with *caṃdra*. As before, the supreme *au ma umaṃ maḥ* consists of five lakhs starting with *sūrya*. As before, the supreme *kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ca eva* consists of six lakhs starting with *skaṃda*. As before, the supreme *ccaṃ ṅaṃ vaṃ* consists of seven lakhs starting with *gaṇeśa*. *Chaṃ jaṃ...* [and so forth].

Jha, ṣṭa, and la—eight hundred thousand times, beginning with Vaṭuka as before, followed by Dha, na, ya, and dva—twelve hundred thousand times, beginning with Vāṇī as before; Pha, ba, and ma—the thirteenth mantra—nine hundred thousand times, beginning with Brahmā as before; Ḍa, ḍha, and ṇa—ten hundred thousand times and so on, beginning with Viṣṇu as before; Ta, tha, da, and me—eleven hundred thousand times, beginning with Śaipā as before;
La—one hundred thousand times, beginning with Lakṣmī as before; Ma, ya, ra, and ca—fourteen hundred thousand times, beginning with Gaurī as before.

Beyond that, one should recite the Laṃvaṃśa fifteen lakhs of times; beyond that, Durgā and others as before; then the Pādyarśa sixteen lakhs of times; and the Tripurā and others consisting of sixteen syllables. This becomes the entirety, with the presiding deity of all mantras, for the sake of bestowing the fruit. O Maheśvarī, the mantra-installation (nyāsa) is declared as "Ambā Devyai Namaḥ," joined with the Sixteen Kūṭeśvarīs, [to be performed] in the Ādhāra, Liṅga, navel, heart, throat, mouth, eyes, and ears.

O Mistress of the Kula, one should place [the mantra] at the cessation, at the half-jujube fruit, at the drop, and at the single digit; likewise in the faces of the intoxicated ones, at the beginning and end of the sound (nāda), and in the region of the Dhruva-maṇḍala. At the end of the three-starred root-mantra, one should place the phrase "consisting of all mantras," followed by "Āyai Parāmbādevyai" and the pervasive [mantra] in the heart. Having thus performed the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa), one should perform the placement of the deities (daivatanyāsa). [The three-starred root...]

At the end of the *lamaṃtra*, one should utter the word "sevita" after "āṃ āṃ sa-srakoṭi-cayogi-kula-śabda. O Dear One, for the *nivṛtti* kalā, one should utter "namaḥ" at the beginning; for the image of the yogin, one should recite the remainder as before. For the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā, one should recite "u ūṃ tapaḥ" and the remainder as before. Likewise, for the *śānti* kalā, one should recite "ṛ ṝṃ śānti" and the remainder as before. For the *śāntyatītā* kalā, one should recite "ḷ ḹṃ muni" and the remainder as before. [Then] "e ai... [and so on].

One should utter "Deva" and the remainder of the syllable *tu*, followed by "Omau" at the end of the word "Rākṣasa," and then "Gagana" as before. [Utter] "Amar" and "Vidyādhara" with the remainder of the syllable *rakta*; "Kaṃ Khaṃ" and "Siddha" with the remainder of the syllable "Mahācchuṣmā"; "Gadya" and "Sādhya" along with "Karālī" and the remainder of the syllable *ṅa* and *ca*; likewise "Apsara" with the remainder of the syllable *ja* and *pa*; "Chaṃ Jaṃ" and "Gandharva" with the remainder of the syllable *vijayā*; "Jhaṃ Jhaṃ" at the end of the word "Guhyaka," and then "Ajitā" as before. [Utter] "Ṭaṃ Ṭhaṃ" and "Pakṣāparājitā" with the remainder of the syllable *ḍa* and *ḍha*.

*Ki* and *nna* for Kinnara-vāmā; the remainder and *ṇa* for Nanta; *pa* and *nnaga* for Jyeṣṭhā; the remainder and *ṇa* for Dhana; *ga* and *ṇe* for Gaṇeśa; *mā* and *yā* for Māyā; the remainder and *pa* and *pha* at the end of the word Bhairava for Kuṇḍalī, as before; *pa* and *ra* and *ba* and *bha* for Vaṭuka-Kālī; the remainder and *ma* and *ya* at the end of the word Kṣetreśa for Kālarātri, as before;

*ra* and *la* for the first Bhagavatī; the remainder and *pū* (0) [as before]; *śa* and *bra* for Brahmā; *sā* and *rve* for Sarveśī; the remainder and *sa* and *vi* for Viṣṇu; *sa* and *rva* for Sarvajñā; the remainder and *ha*. *ṃ*.

O Mistress of the Kula, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the right shoulder down to the left, as follows: [placing] *Laṃ Rudra*, *Sarvakartṛ*, *Īśa*, *Śeṣa*, *Maṃ Yaṃ* at the end of the word *Kṣetrapati*, and *Kālarātri* as before; then *Kṣecarācarā-śakti* and *Śeṣa*. Then, on the two ankles, shanks, knees, thighs, hips, and sides; on the breasts, armpits, shoulders, ears, head, and the opening of the fontanelle (*brahmarandhra*), one should place [the mantras]. At the end of the root mantra consisting of three *Tāras*, [one says] "consisting of the essence of all deities" (*sarvadevātmikā*), and then "for the sake of attainment" (*āyai*).

Having thus performed the pervasive divine placement (*daivanyāsa*) with the heart-mantra of Parāmbā Devī, one should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa as follows: at the end of the three *tāras* and the root mantra, one should recite the groups of consonants (*varga*), followed by "together with the multitude of infinite crores of beings" (*anantakoṭibhūcarīkulasaṃhitāyai*), then *āṃ kṣāṃ*, the word "Saṅgalā," and "to Ambā Devī. Then one should say *āṃ kṣāṃ*, the word "Brahman," then "to Ambā Devī," then "in the multitude of infinite crores of beings" (*anantakoṭibhūtakule*), and finally *saṃhitāyai āṃ kṣaṃ*.

One should utter *Maṅgalanātha* and *Śrī*; then one should pronounce *Bhairavanātha* and *Nam*. One should state the *Ca*-group, *Khecarī*, *Mīlā*, *Carcikā*, and *Maheśvarī*; likewise, *Vetāla*, *Milicarcika*, *Caruru*, and *Śeśa* as before.

One should state the *Ṭha*-group, *Pātālavarī*, *Mū*, *Hāṃ*, *Yogeśvarī*, *Kaumārī*, *Piśāca*, *Ḍaṃhaṃ*, *Vadegeśa*, and *Caṇḍaka*. One should state the *Ta*-group, *Dikcarī*, *Riṃsāha*, and *Rasiddhā*.

*Bāvaiṣṇavī* [is used] for *Apasmāra*; *Ṛiṃsaṃhara-siddha-krodha* and so forth as before; *Pavarga* with *Sahacarī*, *Ḷṃṣāṃ Bhaṭṭinī*, and *Vārāhī* follow; then *Brahmarākṣasa*, *Ḷṃṣaṃ Madhumattā* and so forth as before; *Pavarga* with *Giricarī*, *Aiṃ Śāki-Likile* and so on; *Indrāṇī*, *Ceṭaka*, *Aṃśa*, *Kilikila*, and *Kapālika*; *Śavarga* with *Vanacarī*, *Auṃ Śaṅkalā* and so forth.

*Rātri*, *Cāmuṇḍā*, *Vaṃcakālarātri* (the terrifying), *Lakṣmī* (the aquatic one), and thereafter *Bhīṣaṇā*; *Mahālakṣmī*, *Kūṣmāṇḍā*, and thereafter *Bhīṣaṇā*; and *Saṃhārabhairava*—one should recite the remainder as before.
One should thus perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the root center, the genitals, the navel, the *anāhata*, the *viśuddhi*, the *ājñā*, the forehead, and the *brahmarandhra*.

At the end of the three-syllable root mantra, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) by uttering "Oṃ, obeisance to Mātṛkā-mātṛ-bhairava-adhipati-parāmbā-devī. With a concentrated mind, O Goddess, one who is the lord of the Kula should thus perform the *mātṛ-nyāsa*. Having thus placed the limbs of the body, O Goddess, one whose intellect is focused on no other should meditate upon the Lord: [He is] situated within a grove of Kalpa-trees on a beautiful Golden Island arising in the midst of the ocean of nectar, upon a throne of rubies.

In a pavilion made of the nine precious gems, [he beholds] Him seated upon a lotus on a glorious lion-throne within a triangle, possessing the luster of hundreds of moons and suns; joined with the goddess Umā as His half-body, adorned with distinct ornaments, possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, eternally sixteen years of age,
with a face like a lotus blooming with a gentle smile, three-eyed, moon-crested, clad in divine garments, garlands, and unguents, and adorned with divine jewelry, holding a drinking vessel...

One should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Ardhanārīśvara within the lotus of the heart, holding in his hands the *traṃcaci* mudrā, the trident, and the book, appearing as if manifesting the Goddess of Wisdom (*Vidyā*) while his face and eyes are ever-blissful; he is served by the entire host of deities arisen from the Great Ṣoḍaśa. Or, O Goddess, one may remember him in male form, or contemplate him in female form, or else meditate on him as the partless (*niṣkala*), characterized by Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), consisting entirely of light. One should meditate thus.

Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should display the ten mudrās, which possess both moving and non-moving forms: the Yoni, Liṅga, Surabhi, and Heti mudrās—these four; followed by the Vanamālā, Mahāmudrā, and Namomudrā in succession. One should recite the root mantra as many times as possible, as well as the Śrīpādukā mantra.
One should contemplate the Lord, the Śrī Guru in the form of Śiva, upon a thousand-petaled lotus, [resembling] all the cool rays of the moon...

One should constantly remember on one’s head the Guru, preceded by his name—the one whose lotus-hands grant boons and fearlessness, who possesses pure fragrance, flowers, and excellent raiment, whose face and eyes are serene, and who embodies the form of all deities. O Goddess, when this Nyāsa has been performed in this manner, the practitioner becomes manifest as Paraśiva himself; there is no doubt in this regarding his capacity for both restraint and grace. All the gods [revere] him who performs the Nyāsa known as Mahāṣoḍhā day after day.

O Pārvatī, those who bow down to it—I too bow down to them without doubt—whoever performs this Nyāsa known as the Great Ṣoḍhā (Mahāṣoḍhā), O Goddess, that place is declared to be a divine field extending ten yojanas in all directions. Wherever a man stands after performing this Nyāsa, O Beloved, there he shall attain victory and gain, even if he is an ordinary person. If one who has performed the Mahāṣoḍhā Nyāsa should salute an ignorant person, [the latter] would die within a month.

If Śiva himself is the protector, then those dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, the earth, mountains, waters, and forests—beings with uplifted staffs, Vetālas, gods, Rākṣasas, Grahas, and so forth—as well as all the Devas, Ṛṣis, Yogīs, and lords of Munis, shall [protect him]. O my beloved, what is the use of saying much?
This Nyāsa of mine, O Goddess, one should not tell to one who is not a son, nor should one reveal it to one who is not a disciple. One attains the perfection of command...

One should perform the secret Nyāsa of Pnoti for the sake of attaining the state of the deity who is the protection beyond this; of this there is no doubt in the world—this is the truth, the truth, O fair-faced one. Entry into the Urdhvāmnāya, contemplation upon the Parā-prāsāda, and the thorough knowledge of the Mahāṣoḍhā—these do not yield their fruit for one who lacks [the aforementioned]. Ādinātha is in the Divine Current (Divyaugha), as is his Śakti, Sadāśiva, and his consort Īśvarī.

Bhāryārudra, his slayer Viṣṇu, his beloved Brahmā, and his wife—these twelve are declared in the Divyaugha. Then there are Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra, Sanatsujāta, Ṛbhukṣaja, Dattātreya, Raivataka, Vāmadeva, and after him Vyāsa and Śuka; these eleven are proclaimed in the Mānavaugha. And Nṛsiṃha...

He is Śobhās kara, as well as Mahendra, Mādhava, and Viṣṇu; these six are proclaimed [as the names]. O Goddess, one should join the word "divya" (divine) at the end of the name, and "uccaiḥ paramaṃ śivam" (the supreme, exalted Śiva), and "mahāśivam" (the Great Śiva) in the assembly of Siddhas, and "sadāśivam" (the Eternal Śiva) in the assembly of humans. O Goddess, one should worship the deities in front and the lineage of Gurus; then, having meditated properly upon the three lineages in sequence, one who is free from mental distraction should [worship] with the sixteen services, together with the limbs.

One should worship Śiva along with his retinue using the root mantra (mūla-mantra) and offerings such as sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata). O Mistress of the Kula, listen as I declare the Vaṭu mantra: first the three-fold Tāra (Om), then "Devīputrāya Vaṭukāya," followed by "Nātha" and [the name] ending with "Kapila-jaṭā-bhāra-bhāsura. One should worship the entire assembly of attendants associated with the Great Ṣoḍhā, beginning with the Praṇava (Om) and ending with "Namaḥ," using their respective names.
[The mantra is: *surapiṅgala*, then the word *trinetra*, followed by the word *jvālāmukha*, then the pair *imāṃ pūjāṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa*, and finally *yugapāvakavallabha*.

Thus the mantra of Vaṭuka has been stated with forty-four syllables. Satisfied by the offering of the *bali*, may Vaṭuka, who bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*) and is served by *bhūtas* and *vetālas*, grant me peace eternally. Then [follow] the three *tāras*: *sarvayoginībhyaḥ*.
The word *padaṃ* should come next, followed by *sarvabhūtebhyaḥ*, *sarvabhūtādivarttine*, and then *vaṃdibhyaḥ*, *ḍākinībhyaḥ*, and *śākinībhyaḥ*.
After that, one should say the word *trailokye* and then *vāsinībhyo māṃ vada*. Then the pair *pūjāṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa svāhā*.
This mantra of the Yoginī, O Lord of the Kula, consisting of fifty-one syllables, has been declared. Whosoever the Yoginī may be, even if she is terrible—

May the three Tārās—Khecarī, Bhūcarī, and Vyomacarī—who are even more formidable than the terrible ones and are ever pleased with me, protect me. One should utter the word "to all beings" (*sarvabhūtebhyaḥ*), and after that, the seventeen-syllable heart-mantra (*hṛdukta*) beginning with "to all lords of beings" (*sarvebhūtapatibhyaḥ*). [The mantra continues: "To those of various forms, whether divine, terrestrial, or moving in the atmosphere, or residing in the depths of the netherworld (Pātāla), who are meditated upon through the yoga of the sword; from Dhruva onwards, those of true resolve, and even the Indras."

"May those residing in the eight directions be satisfied with delighted minds; being pleased, may they accept this bali offering. One should utter the three *Tāra*s (Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ), then the pair "Devi-pada" (Oṃ Devi Hūṃ Phaṭ).
Then, for the son Vaṭukanātha, who takes the remnants, one should say the pair "Gṛhṇa" (Accept) and the word "Ruru," followed by the word "Kṣetrapāla.
Then the word "Sarvavighnān" (all obstacles), followed by the pair "Nāśaya" (destroy). [Offer] this worship accompanied by all ritual services (*upacāra*).

O Dear One, one should recite the *vali* mantra for the Kṣetrapāla as follows: "Gṛhṇa-dvayaṃ toyam" (Accept this water-offering twice); this *kṣetrapāla-mantra*, consisting of sixty-four syllables, is said to bestow all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhis*). [The mantra is: "He who dwells in this field, the Kṣetrapāla, the excellent servant—by the offering of this cool water, may he grant me protection from all [dangers].
One should first utter the three *Tāras* (Om Āḥ Hūṃ), then the *Śrī-prāsāda-parā-mantra*: "Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ," followed by "Bhairavādhiṣṭhitāya" at the end.

After *tāyaca akṣobhya* and *ānaṃdataḥ*, one should say *paścāsmidudayābhīṣṭataḥ paraṃ*. Then, for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*), one should utter the word *pada*. After that, the two words *avatara*; then the word *kṣetrapāla*; then the word *mahāśānmahāśāstra*; then the word *mātṛputra*; then the word *kulaputra*; or in this case, the word *siddhaputra*; then *sthānādhipataye*; and then *asmingrāmābhipaye asmi*.
[O] *deśādhipataye*, then *meghanādam*, followed by the word *pracaṇḍogra*. After that, the word *bhīmakṛpāṇam*, and then the word *bhīṣaṇa*.

It should be: *sarvavidyādhipataye imāṃ pūjāṃ valiṃ gṛhṇa*. Then the pair *yugmam*, the pair *muruvargaya*, the pair *yugmam*, the pair *jvala*, the pair *yujvala*, [and the words] "ward off all obstacles" (*sarvavighnaṃ nivāraya*), the pair "destroy" (*nāśaya*), and finally *kṣāṃ kṣāṃ*.
One should utter "Tattvamasi" for Kṣetrapāla, followed by "Vauṣaṭ"; this mantra consists of one hundred and sixty syllables. Afterwards, one should recite the three *tāras*, then:

"O Kṣetrapāla of such-and-such [name], O Rājarājeśvari, accept this worship and this *bali* offering. Following that, with the pair ending in *dvitha*, it is remembered as consisting of twenty-eight syllables.
By this offering of *bali*, may the god Rājarājeśvara, together with his host of attendants, be gracious to me.
O Mistress of the Kula, one should always offer the *vaṭuka* oblation to the west, the *yoginī* oblation to the north, the *bhūta* oblation to the east, and the *kṣetrapāla* oblation to the south;
one should worship Rājarājeśvara with honey. The oblation for *vaṭuka* is prescribed to be offered with the thumb and ring finger;
the oblation for the *yoginīs* with the index, middle, and ring fingers; and the oblation for the *bhūtas*, O Dear One, with all the fingers.
The offering to Kṣetrapāla is made with the thumb and forefinger; that for the King and the Lord of Kings is made with the thumb and middle finger.

Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): there, having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the end of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Brahmā, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Jagatī meter (*chandas*), on the face; salutation to the deity Śrīmad-Ardhanārīśvara, on the heart. Then, the Mahāṣoḍhā-nyāsa is performed.
In Yoga, with palms joined in *añjali*, [one assigns the mantras]: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsauṃḥ śauṃ* to the thumbs, saying "Salutation to Īśāna"; to the index fingers, *hsauṃ śauṃ* to Tatpuruṣa;
to the middle fingers, *hsuṃ śiṃ* to Vāmadeva; to the feet, *hsauṃ śauṃ* to Sadyojāta; to the head, *hsāṃ śauṃ* to Īśāna, the upper face;
to the mouth, *hsesheṃ* to Tatpuruṣa, the eastern face; and to the right ear, *hsushuṃ* to Aghora.
To the southern face: *Hsiṃ* at the left ear; to the northern face, Vāmadeva: *Saṃ* at the left temple; to the western face, Sadyojāta:
*Ni* at the navel. This is the *aṅganyāsa*. One should perform the placement on each face sequentially using the five fingers, beginning with the thumb, assigning one syllable to each finger.
Then, having performed the *ṣaḍaṅganyāsa* on the hands with *Hsāṃ Hsīm*, and so forth, one should meditate upon the God as described in the salutation and perform the placement (*nyāsa*).

Therein, the placement of the expansion of the letters (*prapañcanyāsa*) is as follows: (4) *Hsauḥ Shaiḥ Aṃ*, obeisance to Śrī, whose form is the expansion (*prapañca-rūpā*). (6) *Āṃ*, obeisance to her whose form is the earth (*dvi-parūpā*). (6) *Ī*, obeisance to Kamalā, whose form is the ocean (*jaladhi-rūpā*). (6) *Īṃ*, obeisance to Viṣṇuvallabhā, whose form is the mountain (*giri-rūpā*). (6) *Uṃ*, obeisance to Padmadhāriṇī, whose form is the city (*tana-rūpā*).
