Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Goddess Ambā of the Sixteen Peaks, the presiding deity of all mantras consisting of the sixteen syllables such as Tripurā, which have sixteen million and ten billion divisions," one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with: "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsauṃḥ shauṃḥ aṃ (50), obeisance to the Goddess Śrī Parāmbā, the presiding deity of all mantras; shauṃḥ hsauṃḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ oṃ. This is the mantra-placement (*mantra-nyāsa*). Therein, [the right...]

To the Mother Goddess Nivṛtti, served by a thousand crores of Ṛṣi families, [salutation] on the right foot; to the Mother Goddess Pratiṣṭhā, served by a thousand crores of Yoga families, [salutation] on the left; to the Mother Goddess Vidya, served by a thousand crores of Tapasvi families, [salutation] on the right ankle; to the Mother Goddess Śānti, served by a thousand crores of Nanta families, [salutation] on the left; to the Mother Goddess Śāntyatītā, served by a thousand crores of Brahma families, [salutation] on the right shank. (The sequence continues with the syllables *ḷṃ* and *ḹṃ*.)

To the Goddess Aiśānyatītā, served by thousands of crores of sages: *vāṃ aiṃ aiṃ* to the Goddess Hṛllekhāmbā, served by thousands of crores of divine families; at the right knee: *oṃ auṃ* to the Goddess Gaganāmbā, served by thousands of crores of Rākṣasa families; at the right thigh: *tāṃ eṃ aḥ* to the Goddess Raktāmbā, served by thousands of crores of Vidyādhara families; at the right calf: *ka khaṃ saha*.

To Jayāmbā, served by a thousand koṭis of the Sṛkoṭiprasa family—at the root of the left thigh; to Jayāmbā, served by a thousand koṭis of the Gandharva family—at the right side; to the goddess Ajitāmbā, served by a thousand koṭis of the Guhyaka family—at the left; to the goddess Aparājitāmbā, served by a thousand koṭis of the Yakṣa family—at the right; [to the goddess served by] a thousand koṭis of the Ki... [family]—at the left.

*Thaṃ* on the left shoulder for the Mother Āmbā, who is served by a thousand crores of the *Naraka* lineage; *Daṃ* at the base of the right arm for the Goddess Jyeṣṭhāmbā, who is served by a thousand crores of the *Pitṛ* lineage; *Naṃ* on the left [arm] for the Goddess Māyāmbā, who is served by a thousand crores of the *Gaṇeśvara* lineage; *Paṃ Phaṃ* on the right arm for the *Kuṇḍa* [Mother], who is served by a thousand crores of the *Bhairava* lineage.

To the goddess Ekālyambā, who is served by a thousand koṭis of the Vaṭuka-kula, on the right shoulder; to the goddess Kālarātryambā, who is served by a thousand koṭis of the Kṣetrapāla-kula, on the left shoulder; to the goddess Stavākatyambā, who is served by a thousand koṭis of the Prathama-kula, on the left arm;
to the goddess Sarveśvarī, who is served by a thousand koṭis of the Brahma-kula, on the right ear.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "namas" as follows: to Aryanbādevī on the left shoulder, who is served by a thousand crores of the Viṣṇu lineage; to Sarvajñāmbādevī on the forehead, who is served by a thousand crores of the Rudra lineage; to Sarvakartryambādevī at the *brahmarandhra*, who is served by a thousand crores of the mobile and immobile (*carācara*) lineages; and to Kulaśaktyambādevī [at the heart], saying "namas" to her who is the sovereign of all deities.
"Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ saḥ hauṃ hsauṃḥ śrīparāmbādevyai namaḥ"—one should perform this as the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa); thus ends the deity-placement (daivata-nyāsa).
Now begins the *Mātṛkā-nyāsa*. Therein, at the *mūlādhāra*: (6) *kaṃ* (4). Salutation (*namaḥ*) to the goddess Āṃ Kṣāṃ Maṅgalāmbā, accompanied by infinite crores of the *bhūcarī-kula*;

to the goddess Āṃ Kṣāṃ Brahmāṇyambā, accompanied by infinite crores of the *bhūta-kula*; to Aṃ Kṣaṃ Maṅgala-nātha; and to Aṃ Kṣaṃ Asitāṅga-bhairava. At the *svādhiṣṭhāna*: (6) *caṃ* (4). [Salutation] to the goddess accompanied by infinite crores of the *khecarī-kula*.

To the venerable goddess Īḷārcikāmbā together with her retinue; to the venerable goddess Īḷāmāheśvarī together with her retinue; to the venerable Carcikānātha together with his retinue; to Rurubhairava; in the Maṇipūraka [cakra], Ṭaṃ (4) to the venerable goddess Yogeśvarīmbā together with her retinue of infinite millions of Pātālacarīs;
to the venerable goddess Kaumārīmbā together with her retinue of infinite millions of Piśācas; Hūṃ Hāṃ.

To the Lord Yogeśvara-nātha together with [his] retinue, *uṃ haṃ*; to Caṇḍabhairava, *uṃ haṃ*. In the Anāhata [cakra], *taṃ* (four times); to the Goddess Harasiddhāmbā together with the families of infinite crores of Dikcarīs, *ṛṃ sāṃ*; to the Goddess Vaiṣṇavyambā, *ṛ sāṃ*; to the Lord Harasiddhanātha together with the families of infinite crores of Apasmāras, *ṛṃ saṃ*; to Krodhabhairava, *ṛṃ saṃ*. In the Viśuddha [cakra], *pa* (four times); together with infinite crores...

To Hṛṃ Ṣāṃ Bhaṭṭinyambā Devī, together with the family of infinite crores of Rīkulas; to Hṛṃ Ṣāṃ Varāhyambā Devī; to Ḷṃ Ṣaṃ Bhadinātha, together with the family of infinite crores of Brahma-rākṣasas; to Hṛṃ Ṣaṃ Unmattabhairava. (In the Command [Ājñā], 6: Yaṃ 3. To Aiṃ Śāṃ Kilikilāmbā Devī, together with the family of infinite crores of Giricarīs; to Aiṃ Śāṃ Indrāṇyambā Devī; (together with the family of infinite crores of Ceṭakas).

To the Lord Kili-Kila, together with his retinue of Karmas, *aiṃ śaṃ*; to Kapālibhairava, *aiṃ śaṃ*; on the forehead (*bhāle*), to the Mother Goddess Kālarātri, accompanied by an infinite multitude of forest-dwelling bees, *auṃ vāṃ*; to the Mother Goddess Cāmuṇḍā, accompanied by an infinite multitude of spirits (*preta*), *auṃ vāṃ*; to the Lord Kālaśakti, *auṃ vaṃ*; to Bhīṣaṇabhairava, *auṃ vaṃ*; in the Brahma-aperture (*brahmarandhre*), *laṃ kṣaṃ*, [to] Ananta...

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Mother Goddess Ambā, who is terrifying with her host of ten million aquatic creatures; hāṃ, salutation to the Mother Goddess Mahālakṣmī;
aṃ laṃ, salutation to the Terrifying Lord (*Bhīṣaṇanātha*) accompanied by his host of ten million Kūṣmāṇḍas; aṃ laṃ, salutation to Saṃhārabhairava. Then:
"Aṃ (50), salutation to the venerable Mother Goddess Parāmbā, the presiding deity of all the Mothers and Bhairavas; śauṃḥ hsauḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ."

Saying "Oṃ," one should perform the pervasive placement; this is the Mātṛkā-nyāsa. This concludes the Mahāṣoḍhā-nyāsa. Then, having performed the placement of the hands and the six limbs (kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) as before, and having meditated upon the Lord in His previously described form as one's own nature, one should form the ten mudrās known as the Yoni, Liṅga, Dhenu, Kapāla, Ghaṇṭā, Triśūla, Pustaka, Vanamālā, Namaskāra, and Mahāmudrā. [Then] on the head, Śrīgu...
Having meditated upon the form described in the verse beginning with "In a lotus of a thousand petals," having placed that deity's sandals upon one's head while reciting its mantra,

having prostrated, and having placed one's own secret name at the *mūlādhāra*, one should meditate on the Self as the form of Śiva and remember the previously mentioned greatness of the Mahāṣoḍhā-nyāsa; thus, having performed the Mahāṣoḍhā-nyāsa, [one should perform] the Mūla[-mantra] at the end of the Yogapīṭha-nyāsa.

Having performed three *prāṇāyāmas*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Brahmā, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the *Jagatī* meter on the face; salutation to the deity Śrīmad-Ardhanārīśvara on the heart. Then, having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) with *ha-sāṃ-shīm*, and so forth, and having meditated upon the Lord in the form described for the prostration, one should worship Him with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*). Next, having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus containing a triangle, within that...

Having constructed the worship mandala— consisting of twenty-six petals, outside of which are sixteen petals, outside of that thirty-eight petals, outside of that fourteen petals, and outside of that fifty-one petals, all enclosed by a square— and having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra,

one should perform the placement of the vessels and so forth as before, up to the end of the purifying offerings (puṇyopacāra). Then, having worshipped the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) with "Hsāṃ Hsīṃ" and so forth, [one worships] the triangle...

Having meditated upon the sequence of the teachers of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya)—the divine Siddhas and human [adepts]—situated within the space between the two lotuses by means of the application of unguents, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the first line with the mantra: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ to the divine lineage of teachers known as Parā*.
Then: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ to Ādinātha Paraśiva* (4 times); likewise, *namaḥ to Ādiśakti Paraśivā* (4 times); *namaḥ to Sadāśiva Paraśiva* (4 times); *namaḥ to Sadāśivā*.

Having thus worshipped with "Obeisance to Paraśiva," "Obeisance to Īśvara-Paraśiva," "Obeisance to Īśvarī-Paraśivā," "Obeisance to Rudra-Paraśiva," "Obeisance to Rudrāṇī-Paraśivā," "Obeisance to Viṣṇu-Paraśiva," "Obeisance to Vaiṣṇavī-Paraśivā," and "Obeisance to Brahmāṇī-Paraśivā"—then, on the second line, [one should worship] with:
"Obeisance to the Gurus of the Siddha-lineage, known as Parā"; "Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Sanaka Mahāśiva" (four times).

Salutations to Sanandana Mahāśiva; salutations to Sanātana Mahāśiva; salutations to Sanatkumāra Mahāśiva; salutations to Sanatsujāta Mahāśiva; salutations to Ṛbhu Mahāśiva; salutations to Dattātreya Mahāśiva; salutations to Raivataka Mahāśiva; salutations to Vāmadeva Mahāśiva; salutations to Vyāsa Mahāśiva; salutations to Śuka Mahāśiva—having thus worshipped [them], [one worships] the Mānavaughas upon the third line.

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the gurus known as Parākhya, and having worshipped with the mantras: "Obeisance to Nṛsiṃha-Sadāśiva," "Obeisance to Maheśa-Sadāśiva," "Obeisance to Bhāskara-Sadāśiva," "Obeisance to Mahendra-Sadāśiva," and "Obeisance to Mādhava-Sadāśiva," one should then offer a handful of flowers to the fifty-one-petaled lotus located outside of all [the previous ones], saying: "Obeisance to the fifty-one-petaled lotus. Then...

Beginning from the northeast corner (*devagradala*): *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsauṃḥ shauṃḥ aṃ prapañcarūpāyai śriyai namaḥ*. *Aṃ dvīparūpāyai sāyāyai namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped the fifty-one deities mentioned in the *Prapañcanyāsa* by moving counter-clockwise (*vāmāvartena*), [one should offer] the flower-offering with: *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ hsoṃ shauṃḥ aṃ (50) sakalaprapañcādhidevatāyai parāmbādevyai namaḥ shauṃḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ oṃ*.

Having offered a handful of flowers while reciting the verse beginning with "Having offered the handful of flowers, may there be the attainment of the desired goal," and having prostrated with the words "Salutation to the glorious Ardhanārīśvara, who consists of the deities of the manifest universe," one should then worship with a handful of flowers, saying "Salutation to the fourteen-petaled lotus," beginning from the front of the deity with the mantra "Aṃ Āṃ Iṃ... O Śaktambā, whose abode is the netherworld," and so forth.

Having worshipped this [deity] by means of the counter-clockwise rotation of the fourteen deities mentioned in the *Bhuvananyāsa* with the mantra "O Goddess, to him," (6) having uttered the entire *Mātṛkā*, and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the mantra "Salutation to the venerable goddess Parāmbā, the sovereign of all worlds: *śauṃḥ hsauṃḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ oṃ*," one should offer the worship of the second enclosure as before; then (6), [one worships] "Salutation to the seat of thirty-eight petals."

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and worshipped the thirty-eight deities— beginning with "Oṃ, obeisance to Śavā" and so forth— as prescribed in the *Mūrtinyāsa*, in counter-clockwise order; then, having offered a handful of flowers with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the venerable goddess Parāmbā, who is the essence of the three forms (*trimūrti*), shauṃḥ hsauṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ," and having performed the worship of the third enclosure (*tṛtīyāvaraṇa*) as before, then [the sixth enclosure]...

Having worshipped the ten-petalled lotus seat as before, one should likewise worship the sixteen deities in counter-clockwise order— beginning with *aṃ āṃ īṃ eṃ ekalakṣakoṭibheda* and so forth, and ending with *kakūṭe svaryaṃbā devyai namaḥ*— as prescribed in the *Maṃtranyāsa*. Then,
having worshipped as before with *aṃ (50) sakalamaṃtrādhidevatāyai namaḥ* and *shauṃḥ hsauṃḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ oṃ*, [one should proceed] as before.

Having offered the fourth enclosure (*caturthāvaraṇa*) and presented a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the mantra "Obeisance to the lotus of twenty-six petals" (*ṣaḍviṃśatidalapadmāya namaḥ*), one should worship the twenty-six deities mentioned in the *Devatānyāsa*— beginning with "AṂ ĀṂ SAḤ Obeisance to Nivṛtti, the goddess who bestows boons" (*nivṛtyavaradevyai namaḥ*)— and then, as before, worship the Sovereign of all Deities, the venerable Goddess Parāmbā, with "AṂ Obeisance to Śrī Parāmbā Devī," and [continue] as previously described.

Then, having offered the *camāvaraṇa* (the ground-covering), and having worshipped [it] as before with "Obeisance to the abode of the eight-petaled lotus," one should worship the eight deities mentioned in the *Mātṛkā-nyāsa*, beginning with "Obeisance to Ananta-koṭi-bhūcarī" and ending with "Obeisance to Asitāṅga-Bhairava. Then, [one worships] "Obeisance to all the Mothers and Bhairavas..."

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the mantra "Obeisance to the goddess Śrī Parāmbā, the presiding deity of sound," and having offered the sixth enclosure (*ṣaṣṭhāvaraṇa*) as before,

one should then worship the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and their weapons within the square, perform the incense offering (*dhūpa*) and other rites, and at the conclusion of the daily fire sacrifice (*nityahoma*),
fashion a mandala consisting of a square, a dance-ground (*nṛtta*), and a triangle on the western side of the circle of worship (*pūjācakra*). There, with the *vaṭuka* mantra...

Having invoked him and worshipped him with offerings such as perfumes and other services, one should place there a vessel for the *bali* offering, filled with food, condiments, and water, along with its lid.

Then, using the left thumb and ring finger, one should offer the *arghya* water while reciting the mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ! O Devī-putra Vaṭukanātha, radiant with a mass of tawny matted hair, tawny-eyed, three-eyed, with a flaming mouth, accept, accept this worship and *bali*—svāhā!"

Having offered the *bali* with the *dhārādāna* (continuous stream of water) and having presented a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the mantra beginning with "Oṃ saṃtuṣṭi," one should likewise fashion a maṇḍala with that same [mantra].
Having worshipped there in the same manner with the *yoginī* mantra, one should place the *bali* vessel there as before and [recite]:
*Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sarvayoginībhyaḥ sarvabhūtavartinī-vandinībhyaḥ ḍākinībhyaḥ śākinībhyaḥ trailokya...*

Saying "O you who dwell in the sky, accept, accept this worship and offering, svāhā," one should offer the bali as before with the left hand’s index, middle, and ring fingers in the shape of a *yoni*. Then, having offered a handful of flowers with the mantra "Whosoever the Yoginī, O Terrible One" (*yā kācid yoginī ghoreti*), and then having likewise prepared the maṇḍala as before, one should worship there with perfumes and other offerings using the mantra for all spirits (*sarvabhūta-mantra*) as previously described.

Having placed the *bali* vessel there, one should offer the *bali* as before with the fingers while reciting the mantra "Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sarvabhūtebhyaḥ sarvabhūtapatibhyo namaḥ," and having offered a handful of flowers with the mantra "To the spirits of various forms," one should then likewise prepare a mandala on the right side, worship Kṣetrapāla there with his mantra, and place the *bali* vessel as before.

Reciting the mantra: *dhāya oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ dehi dehi devīputrāya vaṭutāthāya ucchiṣṭahāriṇe gṛhṇa gṛhṇa rurukṣetrapāla sarva-vighnān nāśaya sarvopacāra-sahitām imāṃ pūjāṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā*, one should offer the *bali* as before with the left thumb and forefinger, saying: "And he who dwells in this field... and so forth.

Having offered three handfuls of flowers (*trepuṣpāñjali*), or else: *Aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ hsauṃḥ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ*, [I invoke] the Kṣetrapāla presided over by Bhairava, the son of the Mother, the son of the Clan, the son of the Siddhas—Akṣobhya Nandodaya—for the sake of attaining my desired success: descend, descend upon this Lord of the Place, this Lord of the Village, this Lord of the Region, O Megha!
To the Lord of all obstacles, who is terrifying and formidable with a fierce sword made of intense sound—accept, accept this worship and this *bali* offering!

*Ruru muru, crush, crush, blaze, blaze, burn brightly, burn brightly; ward off all obstacles, destroy, destroy!* With the mantra ending in *kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣetrapālāya vauṣaṭ huṃ*, one should offer the *bali* as before.

In the south-eastern corner, having invoked Rājarājeśvara within the eastern maṇḍala and worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings, one should place the vessel for the bali offering there as before.

Then, reciting the mantra "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Amuka-kṣetrapāla Rājarājeśvara, accept this worship, accept this bali, Svāhā!", one should offer the bali by pouring a stream of water from the arghya-vessel using the thumb and middle finger. Thus it is concluded.
Having offered a handful of flowers with the mantra "navalidāneti," one should complete the remaining rites, such as the *nīrājana* ceremony, as previously described.

Likewise, O Beloved, the practitioner, with a purified heart and observing the aforementioned rules, should mutter the supreme *Śrīprāsāda* mantra according to its true essence. O Goddess, he should perform oblations in the consecrated fire in a quantity equal to one-tenth of the recitation, using perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and the *kalpa-dhenu*.

O beloved Kulanāyikā, one should satisfy the circle of Yoginīs with garments and other gifts, as well as with various kinds of food, drink, and delightful family heirlooms, according to the extent of one's wealth. Thus, O Goddess, through the placement of mantras (nyāsa), recitation (japa), meditation (dhyāna), fire-offerings (homa), worship (arcana), and libations (tarpaṇa), the practitioner who has mastered the mantra becomes manifest as Paraśiva himself. Thereafter, O Mistress of the Kula, one may perform the desired ritual applications (prayoga) by means of the mantra according to one's own tradition.

Therefore, one should accomplish this *Atimānsā* for the sake of both enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). For one whose mantra is perfected, the six rites (*ṣatkarma*) will undoubtedly succeed;

however, they do not succeed for one who has not perfected it, and such a person shall not attain the grace of the deity. For those who perform rites for selfish desires, there is no attainment in the next world;
their success in practice yields only another fruit elsewhere, O Beloved. There is never a double result from even a single ritual procedure.

Therefore, one who is free from desire should worship the deity; through oblations (*homa*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), yantras, and the like born of specific meditations, one should perform the six rites (*ṣatkarma*) for both oneself and others. At the conclusion of the ritual application (*prayoga*), one should perform the worship of the *cakra* according to the lunar day (*tithi*).

Thus, accompanied by meditation and ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times to pacify any defects in the ritual application. For the sake of one's own [purification],...

This is for the sake of protection; otherwise, one would not obtain the fruit [of the rite] but would incur the curse of the deities. Having understood the lunar day (*tithi*), weekday (*vāra*), asterism (*ṛkṣa*), and *karana*, as well as the conjunctions (*yoga*), month, season (*ṛtu*), and fortnight (*pakṣa*), along with the diagrams of the lords of the continents (*dvīpeśa*) and the tortoise (*kūrma-cakra*), one should accomplish the ritual acts. Having understood the five purifications (*pañca-śuddhi*), the seat (*āsana*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the placement of mantras (*mantra-nyāsa*), the rosary (*akṣamālikā*), the defects, the consecration (*saṃskāra*), and the mudrās, one should accomplish the mantras.

Having understood the compatibility of the letters of the zodiac signs known as enemies, kinsmen, and wives, as well as the friendship of the elements from beginning to end, one should practice the mantras.

Having understood the distinctions between mantra and vidyā, sleep and awakening, the forms of fire and moon, and [the nature of] male, female, and neuter, one should practice the mantras. Furthermore, having understood the connection between the name, the direction, the letters, the nāḍīs, and the principles (tattvas), as well as the deity, time, mudrās, and so forth—

One should accomplish the rites to be performed; having understood the five substances for writing, the location, and the dimensions of the yantras, one should accomplish the yantras. Having understood the origin, the mercury, the color, the form, the consecration, and the arrangement, as well as the dimensions of the sacrificial pit and the materials, one should perform the homa. [One should observe] the radiance of the abode, the smoke, the sound, the fragrance, the blessing, the shape, and the gestures of the messenger.

Having understood [the nature of] the auspicious and inauspicious, one should speak; having understood the contemplation of the reality of mantras (*mantra-tattva-anusaṃdhāna*), the characteristics such as the possession of the body (*dehāveśa*), and the various methods of mantra utterance (*saṃtroccāraṇa-bheda*), one should accomplish the mantras. Having understood the mandala, the decoction of time and power (*kāla-śakti-kvātha*), water, the eight perfumes (*gandhāṣṭaka*), and so forth, as well as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the bestowing of names, one should perform the initiation. [One should also understand] the daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites, the observances (*niyama*), and the latent impressions of names (*nāma-vāsanā*).

Having understood the worship, the dhāraṇī-mantras, the yantras, and so forth, one should accomplish the rites. Having understood the entry into the house of worship and other matters, the characteristics of the family-worshipper (kulapūjaka), and the attainment of the family-substances (kuladravya) and so on, one should perform the worship. Regarding internal sacrifice (antaryāga), external sacrifice (bahiryāga), the water-offering (arghya) and so forth, the libations (tarpaṇa), the svāhā-utterance, and the nyāsa—whatever is prescribed for the time of recitation, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should join those [elements] at the end of the mantra during the time of japa.

For propitiatory rites (*śāntika*), silver or copper [is used]; for subjugation (*vaśyaka*), birch-bark; for all purposes, gold; and for cruel rites (*krūra*), a cloth from a corpse. For propitiatory rites, the three fragrances are prescribed; for subjugation, the five fragrances; for all purposes, the [five] fragrances; and for cruel rites, the eight poisons. For propitiatory rites, *leṣanī* and *dūrvā* grass [are used]; for subjugation and the like, a peacock feather; for all purposes, gold; and for cruel rites, a crow.

O Dear One, having learned from the mouth of the Guru the characteristics of the *pichikā* (the ritual vessel), the pacifying rite (*śāntika*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and so forth—performed in the temple of Caṇḍikā for all rites, or in a temple or cremation ground for cruel rites (*krūra-karma*)—the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) should perform all rites to obtain their fruit.
At the base is the seed-syllable of the temple (*prāsāda-bīja*), resembling the color of the dawn; at the top of the head is the supreme seed-syllable (*parā-bīja*), like the moon.

One should constantly contemplate oneself from head to foot as being sprinkled by the nectar-essence, which flows in an unbroken stream from the base to the *brahmarandhra*, filled with the intensity of bliss ignited by the mutual touch of hands, possessing a radiant luster like lightning. O Goddess, having understood the installation, worship, and the five-fold handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjali*), one should perform the ritual of worship, beginning with the vessel, its support, and so forth, including the offering of meat.
O Mistress of the Kula, having understood the *kulamelanatarpaṇa*, the *vaṭukādivali*, and the worship, one should perform the rite;

and having understood the distinction between the powers known as *kulā* and *akulā*, their characteristics, the auspicious marks [of a consort], the consecration and worship of the woman, and the time for union with the Goddess, one should accept a *śakti*. Thus have some specific details been told, O Leader of the Kula.

The procedure for all mantras follows this common sequence: mantras ending in *phaṭ* have male deities and awaken when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is in the right [channel]; vidyās ending in *svāhā* (dviṭh) have female deities, O Dear One, and awaken in the left channel; mantras ending in *namaḥ* have neuter deities and awaken when the breath has entered both channels; and peaceful mantras bring about tranquility.

For the majority [of rites], the mantras should be devoted to immortality (amṛta) and end with *svāhā*. For rites pertaining to the sky (*viyat*) and Agni, they should be used directly; in cruel rites, *phaṭ* should be uttered. In cases of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), *ṭeṭe vaṣaṭ*; in hatred (*dveṣa*) and killing (*māraṇa*), *huṃ*; in paralyzing (*staṃbhana*), *manaḥ* is prescribed; and for pacifying (*śāntika*) and nourishing (*pauṣṭika*) rites, *svāhā* is said. By meditating thus on the Mistress of the Kula (*Kuleśānī*), one becomes ageless and immortal; having meditated thus, one should accomplish all rites, and they will be swiftly perfected.

O Goddess, there is no need for deliberation regarding the performance of the divine dance; O Beloved, I shall now describe the various types of meditation (*dhyāna*) which bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*). By means of this, one obtains one’s desired goal even without ritual worship, fire-offerings (*homa*), and the like. O Goddess, the practitioner (*sādhaka*), with a steady mind, should sit upon a soft seat in a secluded place and meditate after first saluting the Guru. He should meditate upon the Śrī-prāsāda [the Palace of Śrī] situated in the center of the full orb of the moon resting upon his head.

O Beloved, one should meditate upon oneself with a steady inner self as being joined with the sixteen vowels which are the supreme seed-syllables (*parābīja*), white as pearl, crystal, camphor, the *kunda* flower, and the moon, with a body bathed in nectar produced from the orb of the moon. O Dear One, accompanied by youthful radiance, one should recite the supreme mantra of the Śrī-prāsāda one thousand and eight times within the maṇḍala; [this wards off] untimely death.

Having conquered the fear born of disease, old age, and death, as well as the fear arising from planetary afflictions, epilepsy, vetālas, spirits, and insanity, one shall live for more than a hundred years, free from mental and physical ailments, endowed with sons and grandsons, and honored by all mankind. One will understand even unheard scriptures, and one's poetic composition shall become stainless; such a person is truly born as [the deity] Citā—of this there is no doubt. [Fever, insanity...]

One should mutter [the mantra] while sprinkling water on the head for heart disease; likewise, when afflictions such as colic, wind-disorders, wounds, tumors, or urinary distress arise, one should mutter it while contemplating [the deity] in those very locations, O Lord of Gods, just as before. When great diseases have arisen throughout all the limbs, one should contemplate [the deity] there;
at that moment, all diseases will attain pacification, without a doubt. He who meditates upon [the deity] in the ten sense organs shall obtain the excellence of those senses.

One should remember the *travīja* there; its fruit will certainly come to pass. One should always contemplate it upon the crown of the head, and one shall become free from old age and death. O Dear One, one should know that it is the destroyer of all diseases and the state of health itself. There is no meditation higher than this; it is the truth, without a doubt. O Goddess, this fruit born of *sāttvika* meditation has been declared. One should accomplish pacifying rites (*śāntikarma*) through this method of meditation according to the prescribed rule.

He who meditates upon the seed-syllable conjoined with the twelve vowels within the twelve supporting lotuses (*ādhāra-padmāni*) shall become free from old age and death. One should meditate upon the seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels within the six supporting centers; O Mistress of the Kula, one is then worshipped by the goddesses residing in those six supports. In the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus, situated within a solar disc, is the seed-syllable of the supreme *Prāsāda*, which is as red as the rising sun—O Jayā!

O Ambikā, one should meditate upon oneself with an unwavering inner self as blazing with the luster of gold, vermilion, and rubies, encircled by the twenty-five letters of touch, which—by the shadow of their mass of radiance—have turned the three worlds into jewels.

O Goddess, the wise one should recite one thousand and eight times that supreme seed-mantra of grace (*prasāda-bīja*), endowed with the effulgence of youth, within the maṇḍala. [The gods and demons...]

O beloved, by remembering and reciting [this mantra] upon his head, one undoubtedly brings under control the Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Guhyakas, Kinnaras, Mucukundas, Yakṣas, and other women; as well as lions, tigers, elephants, and other wild beasts. How much more so, then, humans and the like? One attains great sovereignty and enjoyments such as those of heaven; indeed, whoever remembers and recites it upon the head becomes submissive.
O Goddess, this fruit born of meditation on Tejīrā has been proclaimed. By this method, one should accomplish all rites of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*).

O Goddess, it brings about the subjugation of all and shines with the fruit of all sovereignty. There is no meditation superior to this; it is the truth, there is no doubt. [One should meditate on] the seed-syllable of Parā-Prāsāda situated within the fire-mandala in the midst of the lotus of the *mūlādhāra*, ending with the letter *ka* (the fire at the end of time).

Equal in radiance, thoroughly pervaded by the ten pervasive syllables in reverse order, he himself spoke: "O Fire, you who cause fear to all beings, whose face is turned toward the southern quarter, with fierce fangs and a soiled body, endowed with the bloom of youth, one should recite the mantra known as Parā-prāsāda one thousand and eight times within the mandala; it causes strife for those beings who act against one's interests."

O Pārvatī, one should contemplate those who perform evil deeds, who cause vain enmity, who are cruel, and who create obstacles to worship—namely, the Bhūtas, fierce Grahas, Vetālas, Piśācas, and Brahma-rākṣasas—as having fallen into that fire and being consumed by it; in an instant they meet their destruction like deer before a lion. O Lord of Devas, he upon whose head one remembers the seed-syllable (bīja) attains death through this meditation.

O Dear One, this destroys even the most stubborn [obstacles] and brings about the destruction of malevolent influences such as planetary afflictions and diseases. O Goddess, there is no meditation superior to this; this is the truth, of this there is no doubt. O Goddess, I have described this fruit born of *tāmasa* meditation. By means of this rite, one should accomplish the work of slaying the wicked. O Dear One, having learned these various types of meditation from the mouth of the Guru, one should employ the six rites (*ṣatkarma*).
O you who are praised by heroes, victory is attained otherwise [only] through the excellent sacrificial fuels (samidh) of *khadira*, white *mandāra*, *amṛtā*, and *bhānu*;
with the best of *panasa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *ayāma*, and *mārga*; with *nandyāvarta*, white lotuses, *bhaya*, *adrika*, flowers, and other white, auspicious substances;
with *śamī* wood, seasonal fruits, various foods, *durvā* grass, clarified butter, sesame, and rice, along with the three sweets (*madhuratrika*).

O Mistress of the Kula, one who knows the mantras should perform this rite with either a single person or with all [the practitioners], according to the gravity or lightness of the task. O Goddess, the recitation (*jāpya*) should be performed one thousand times, or three thousand, or five thousand; or ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or even a million times, O Mistress of Kula.

Having invoked the deity along with the retinue into this consecrated sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) where the fire has been prepared, and having meditated upon them, O Beloved, one should offer oblations according to the rules.

O Goddess, with an inner self absorbed in this, all suffering born of every disease, fever, insanity, epilepsy, plague, and possession shall be pacified in an instant; of this there is no doubt. By this, O Beloved, there is total peace, and one shall obtain learning and knowledge. [One should offer flowers] born of the kadamba, aśoka, śoka, vakula, punnāga, nameru, madhuka, the two types of campaka, pālāśa, pāṭala, śrī, kapittha, and mālatī.

The best of those who know mantras, knowing the ritual procedure, should offer oblations as before to the deity with auspicious red substances— mallikā, jātī, bandhūka, red lotuses, white water-lilies (kalhāra), red mandāra, jātī, kunda, japā, and other such flowers— as well as with sacrificial wood, parched grain, fruits, and seasonal offerings. He should likewise [offer to] kings, men proud of their beauty and youth, lions, rutting elephants, tigers, serpents, and even wicked beasts.

By means of this, one would surpass the wives of the *ṛddhi*-deities, *apsarases*, *yakṣas*, *gandharvas*, and even the lords of the divine clans; of this there is no doubt. By the oblation of *rājīlava* flowers, one will certainly attract three women. O Lord of Devas, through various substances such as turmeric and the like, with fuel-sticks made of seasonal fruits, along with house-soot, charcoal, the three fires, and collyrium— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. Having ground together the dust from the feet of the person to be subdued (sādhya), mixed with ashes from a funeral pyre, and thoroughly saturated with the *unmatta* juice,

one should fashion an image of the sādhya from the wood of a tree corresponding to his birth-star (*nakṣatra*). Having properly consecrated it with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the practitioner should suspend it above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a darkened mind and, according to the prescribed rite, dig up the clay image beneath the pit in a fierce manner.

One who possesses the highest knowledge of mantras, being intolerant and viewing [the enemy] with an eye of wrath, should offer oblations into the funeral fire kindled by the wood of the *viṣatara* tree using those very substances, just as prescribed for the rites of the gods;

he would undoubtedly perform acts of inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*). O Goddess, in rites of pacification (*śāntika*) one should contemplate the deity as white in color and of a sattvic nature; for subjugation (*vaśya*), O Goddess, one should contemplate the deity as red in color and of a rajasic nature. First, one should perform protection for oneself.

Having performed the subsequent rites, one should accomplish [the goal]; one should meditate upon the Tamasic [form] as dark-complexioned, O Goddess. If one performs it otherwise out of delusion, he becomes a beast for the deity; therefore, O wise one, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the Goddess, one should offer the oblation (*bali*).
Having performed the rites, O you who are praised by heroes, one should act, not otherwise. One should draw a triangle, a hexagon, and an eight-spoked [wheel] on the ground.

O Parameśvarī, one should write the root mantra (mūlamantra) in the center, accompanied by the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (sādhyanāma). O Pārvatī, one should write the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in the six corners; the eight vowels in the filaments (keśara), and the [consonant] groups (varga) in the petals (patra). O Ambikā, one should write the root mantra within the four corners of the earth-palace (bhūgṛha) using powders of five colors, making it auspicious and pleasing to the sight. Thus, one should draw the yantra according to the rules, O Mantra.

O Dear One, the most excellent of practitioners should place twenty-two jars in sequence, beginning from the center and ending with the four corners of the square—specifically one, three, six, ten, and four jars, O Beloved.

Alternatively, O Goddess, on each of the eight petals, one may arrange ten, seven, four, or even a single jar according to the capacity of the practitioner. [The following are the materials: unstable substances, gems, hair, threads, clay, flesh, blood, water, skin, clothing, and the tuft of hair.

Having placed a coconut fruit upon the head [of the vessel], one should recite the mantra endowed with the vital breath (*prāṇa*). One should worship the deity of the jar (*kalaśa-devatā*) together with the three forms (*trimūrti*), the *Aṃśātimātṛs*, and the *Bhairavas*.

O Dear One, having worshipped according to the rules in the intermediate directions the Guru, Vighneśa, Durgā, and Kṣetrapati within the jars, the most excellent knower of mantras should consecrate his dear disciple for the pacification of all sins and for long life.

One shall obtain beauty, splendor, good fortune, knowledge, health, and so forth; an anointed king obtains the earth bounded by the four oceans, and even one who possesses nothing, when consecrated, attains great sovereignty. A barren woman, when consecrated, obtains a son endowed with all virtues. Possessions, untimely death, diseases, and other such evils are destroyed—of this there is no doubt—whether performed on three metals or on birch bark.

O Goddess, having written this supreme yantra and wearing it on the arm, it shall provide total protection. Longevity, health, sovereignty, the attainment of knowledge, fame, victory, and the grace of the Supreme—one who knows the mantra perceives these; there is no doubt in this matter. What is the use of saying more? Among the practitioners of mantra in the three worlds, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by this King of Mantras, according to the singular Upper Tradition (Urdhvāmnāya).

O Kuleśvarī, one who is bathed [in purity], who knows the mantra of the supreme *Prāsāda*, who understands the true meaning of the *Kulārṇava*, and who is liberated while living— whether dwelling in a sacred place,
a non-sacred place, or even in the midst of people— that knower of the supreme *Prāsāda* mantra is undoubtedly liberated.
Following the procedure taught in the Āgamas, preceded by the sequential worship (*kramapūjā*), one should recite the supreme seed-mantra of the venerable *Prāsāda* one hundred and eight times.
O Goddess, he is liberated from the five great sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin; he who recites two hundred times the Śrīprāsāda Parā mantra,

even with eighty-four lakhs of bodily postures, practices, and observances— whether performed in youth, middle age, or old age, during waking, dreaming, or deep sleep, and whether through action, mind, or speech, knowingly or unknowingly— becomes free from the countless karmas accumulated throughout his life.

O fair-faced one, there is no doubt that one is liberated even from the multitudes of great sins (mahāpātaka) and the heaps of minor offenses (upapātaka); this is the truth. O Goddess, he who should mutter three hundred times the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda—whatever merit is found in all sacrifices, whatever fruit in all gifts, whatever merit in all vows, and whatever fruit in all sacred fords (tīrtha)—that fruit he obtains, O Goddess; there is no doubt in this matter.

Whoever constantly recites four hundred times the *Śrīprāsāda-parā-mantra* along with the *Ṛyāvicāraṇā*, the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*) will serve at the door of his house; of this there is no doubt. Endowed with all accomplishments, whatever he desires in his mind, that he shall obtain without a doubt. Virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation—these stand directly in the palm of his hand. [Sālokya...]

O Mistress of the Kula, I am unable to describe the fruit obtained by one who recites the supreme Śrīprāsāda mantra five hundred times— that which bestows the fourfold liberation. Therefore, with every effort, in all circumstances, and at all times,
one should recite the Śrīprāsāda mantra for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
